CHAPTER XII.


As Elinor and Marianne were walking together the next morning the
latter communicated a piece of news to her sister, which in spite of
all that she knew before of Marianne’s imprudence and want of thought,
surprised her by its extravagant testimony of both. Marianne told her,
with the greatest delight, that Willoughby had given her a horse, one
that he had bred himself on his estate in Somersetshire, and which was
exactly calculated to carry a woman. Without considering that it was
not in her mother’s plan to keep any horse, that if she were to alter
her resolution in favour of this gift, she must buy another for the
servant, and keep a servant to ride it, and after all, build a stable
to receive them, she had accepted the present without hesitation, and
told her sister of it in raptures.

“He intends to send his groom into Somersetshire immediately for it,”
she added, “and when it arrives we will ride every day. You shall share
its use with me. Imagine to yourself, my dear Elinor, the delight of a
gallop on some of these downs.”

Most unwilling was she to awaken from such a dream of felicity to
comprehend all the unhappy truths which attended the affair; and for
some time she refused to submit to them. As to an additional servant,
the expense would be a trifle; Mama she was sure would never object to
it; and any horse would do for _him;_ he might always get one at the
park; as to a stable, the merest shed would be sufficient. Elinor then
ventured to doubt the propriety of her receiving such a present from a
man so little, or at least so lately known to her. This was too much.

“You are mistaken, Elinor,” said she warmly, “in supposing I know very
little of Willoughby. I have not known him long indeed, but I am much
better acquainted with him, than I am with any other creature in the
world, except yourself and mama. It is not time or opportunity that is
to determine intimacy;—it is disposition alone. Seven years would be
insufficient to make some people acquainted with each other, and seven
days are more than enough for others. I should hold myself guilty of
greater impropriety in accepting a horse from my brother, than from
Willoughby. Of John I know very little, though we have lived together
for years; but of Willoughby my judgment has long been formed.”

Elinor thought it wisest to touch that point no more. She knew her
sister’s temper. Opposition on so tender a subject would only attach
her the more to her own opinion. But by an appeal to her affection for
her mother, by representing the inconveniences which that indulgent
mother must draw on herself, if (as would probably be the case) she
consented to this increase of establishment, Marianne was shortly
subdued; and she promised not to tempt her mother to such imprudent
kindness by mentioning the offer, and to tell Willoughby when she saw
him next, that it must be declined.

She was faithful to her word; and when Willoughby called at the
cottage, the same day, Elinor heard her express her disappointment to
him in a low voice, on being obliged to forego the acceptance of his
present. The reasons for this alteration were at the same time related,
and they were such as to make further entreaty on his side impossible.
His concern however was very apparent; and after expressing it with
earnestness, he added, in the same low voice,—“But, Marianne, the horse
is still yours, though you cannot use it now. I shall keep it only till
you can claim it. When you leave Barton to form your own establishment
in a more lasting home, Queen Mab shall receive you.”

This was all overheard by Miss Dashwood; and in the whole of the
sentence, in his manner of pronouncing it, and in his addressing her
sister by her Christian name alone, she instantly saw an intimacy so
decided, a meaning so direct, as marked a perfect agreement between
them. From that moment she doubted not of their being engaged to each
other; and the belief of it created no other surprise than that she, or
any of their friends, should be left by tempers so frank, to discover
it by accident.

Margaret related something to her the next day, which placed this
matter in a still clearer light. Willoughby had spent the preceding
evening with them, and Margaret, by being left some time in the parlour
with only him and Marianne, had had opportunity for observations,
which, with a most important face, she communicated to her eldest
sister, when they were next by themselves.

“Oh, Elinor!” she cried, “I have such a secret to tell you about
Marianne. I am sure she will be married to Mr. Willoughby very soon.”

“You have said so,” replied Elinor, “almost every day since they first
met on High-church Down; and they had not known each other a week, I
believe, before you were certain that Marianne wore his picture round
her neck; but it turned out to be only the miniature of our great
uncle.”

“But indeed this is quite another thing. I am sure they will be married
very soon, for he has got a lock of her hair.”

“Take care, Margaret. It may be only the hair of some great uncle of
_his_.”

“But, indeed, Elinor, it is Marianne’s. I am almost sure it is, for I
saw him cut it off. Last night after tea, when you and mama went out of
the room, they were whispering and talking together as fast as could
be, and he seemed to be begging something of her, and presently he took
up her scissors and cut off a long lock of her hair, for it was all
tumbled down her back; and he kissed it, and folded it up in a piece of
white paper; and put it into his pocket-book.”

For such particulars, stated on such authority, Elinor could not
withhold her credit; nor was she disposed to it, for the circumstance
was in perfect unison with what she had heard and seen herself.

Margaret’s sagacity was not always displayed in a way so satisfactory
to her sister. When Mrs. Jennings attacked her one evening at the park,
to give the name of the young man who was Elinor’s particular
favourite, which had been long a matter of great curiosity to her,
Margaret answered by looking at her sister, and saying, “I must not
tell, may I, Elinor?”

This of course made every body laugh; and Elinor tried to laugh too.
But the effort was painful. She was convinced that Margaret had fixed
on a person whose name she could not bear with composure to become a
standing joke with Mrs. Jennings.

Marianne felt for her most sincerely; but she did more harm than good
to the cause, by turning very red and saying in an angry manner to
Margaret,

“Remember that whatever your conjectures may be, you have no right to
repeat them.”

“I never had any conjectures about it,” replied Margaret; “it was you
who told me of it yourself.”

This increased the mirth of the company, and Margaret was eagerly
pressed to say something more.

“Oh! pray, Miss Margaret, let us know all about it,” said Mrs.
Jennings. “What is the gentleman’s name?”

“I must not tell, ma’am. But I know very well what it is; and I know
where he is too.”

“Yes, yes, we can guess where he is; at his own house at Norland to be
sure. He is the curate of the parish I dare say.”

“No, _that_ he is not. He is of no profession at all.”

“Margaret,” said Marianne with great warmth, “you know that all this is
an invention of your own, and that there is no such person in
existence.”

“Well, then, he is lately dead, Marianne, for I am sure there was such
a man once, and his name begins with an F.”

Most grateful did Elinor feel to Lady Middleton for observing, at this
moment, “that it rained very hard,” though she believed the
interruption to proceed less from any attention to her, than from her
ladyship’s great dislike of all such inelegant subjects of raillery as
delighted her husband and mother. The idea however started by her, was
immediately pursued by Colonel Brandon, who was on every occasion
mindful of the feelings of others; and much was said on the subject of
rain by both of them. Willoughby opened the piano-forte, and asked
Marianne to sit down to it; and thus amidst the various endeavours of
different people to quit the topic, it fell to the ground. But not so
easily did Elinor recover from the alarm into which it had thrown her.

A party was formed this evening for going on the following day to see a
very fine place about twelve miles from Barton, belonging to a
brother-in-law of Colonel Brandon, without whose interest it could not
be seen, as the proprietor, who was then abroad, had left strict orders
on that head. The grounds were declared to be highly beautiful, and Sir
John, who was particularly warm in their praise, might be allowed to be
a tolerable judge, for he had formed parties to visit them, at least,
twice every summer for the last ten years. They contained a noble piece
of water; a sail on which was to form a great part of the morning’s
amusement; cold provisions were to be taken, open carriages only to be
employed, and every thing conducted in the usual style of a complete
party of pleasure.

To some few of the company it appeared rather a bold undertaking,
considering the time of year, and that it had rained every day for the
last fortnight;—and Mrs. Dashwood, who had already a cold, was
persuaded by Elinor to stay at home.

The following morning, as Elinor and Marianne strolled through the garden, the younger sister burst forth with news that struck Elinor with genuine astonishment. Despite her deep knowledge of Marianne's impulsiveness, this revelation exceeded even her expectations, revealing a depth of imprudence she had not fully anticipated. With radiant joy, Marianne announced that Willoughby had gifted her a horse—a magnificent animal he had bred himself on his Somersetshire estate, perfectly suited to a lady's needs. She spoke of the gift in raptures, utterly failing to consider that her mother, Mrs. Dashwood, had no intention of keeping horses, nor the practical necessities involved: purchasing a second mount for a servant, hiring an attendant, and constructing a stable. Yet, having already decided to accept, she shared the delight with her sister, envisioning daily rides across the downs.

"You shall share its use with me," Marianne insisted, her eyes alight with dreams of galloping freedom. "Imagine the sheer delight!"

Elinor, however, found it difficult to remain immersed in such a vision of happiness without confronting the harsh realities beneath the surface. For a fleeting moment, she hoped to persuade Marianne that the expense of an extra servant, the inconvenience of housing a horse against her mother's wishes, and the general impropriety of accepting such a generous gift from a man so recently known would dissuade her. But Marianne grew impatient with these practical objections.

"You are mistaken, Elinor," she declared warmly, her tone defensive. "I do not know Willoughby poorly. Though our acquaintance is short, I understand him better than anyone else in the world save you and Mother. Intimacy is not measured by time or opportunity, but by disposition alone. Seven years could pass without two souls knowing one another, yet seven days may suffice for others. To refuse this gift would be far more improper than to accept it from Willoughby."

Realizing that opposing Marianne on such a tender subject would only strengthen her resolve, Elinor shifted her strategy. She appealed to Marianne's love for her mother, painting a vivid picture of the trouble and discomfort this addition would bring upon the gentlewoman who had raised them. Slowly, the storm within Marianne subsided. She promised not to mention the offer to her mother and vowed to decline it politely the next time she saw Willoughby. True to her word, when Willoughby visited the cottage later that day, Elinor heard Marianne express her regret in a hushed voice, explaining the difficulties that forced her hand. Her reasons were presented with such conviction that further persuasion became impossible. Willoughby's distress was palpable; he spoke earnestly of his sorrow, adding in a low, intimate murmur, "But, Marianne, the horse remains yours, though you cannot use it now. I shall keep it until you need it again. When you finally establish your own home, away from Barton, Queen Mab awaits you."

These words, whispered clearly enough for Elinor to overhear, coupled with Willoughby's familiar address of "Marianne" instead of "Miss Dashwood," sent a chill through her heart. In an instant, the nature of their relationship became undeniable to her. There was no ambiguity in his tone or in the terms of his promise; they were clearly engaged. What surprised Elinor was not the engagement itself, but how two people of such frank natures could allow themselves to reach this stage without a single word spoken aloud to the outside world.

Her suspicions were confirmed the following day by Margaret. After Willoughby had spent the previous evening with them, leaving the three of them alone in the parlor, Margaret had observed much. Now, with a grave and conspiratorial expression, she confided in Elinor. "Oh, Elinor!" she exclaimed. "I have a secret to tell you about Marianne. I am certain she will be married to Mr. Willoughby very soon."

"You have said so," Elinor replied dryly, "almost every day since they first met on High-church Down. We had not known each other a week before you were convinced Marianne wore his miniature around her neck; yet it turned out to be merely the likeness of our great-uncle."

"But this is entirely different!" Margaret protested, her eyes wide. "He possesses a lock of her hair."

"Eh?" Elinor feigned surprise. "Take care, Margaret. It may simply be a lock of hair from some great-uncle of *his*."

"But truly, Elinor, it is Marianne's!" Margaret insisted, recounting the scene from the previous night with dramatic flair. "Last evening, after tea, when you and Mother stepped out, they were whispering frantically. He seemed to beg something of her, and then he snatched up her scissors. He cut off a long tangle of hair from behind her ear, kissed it reverently, folded it into a white square of paper, and tucked it safely into his pocket-book."

Given the weight of Margaret's testimony and its alignment with what Elinor had witnessed herself, she could not withhold her full belief in the facts.

Yet, Margaret's sharp tongue occasionally betrayed a lack of tact. Later, when Mrs. Jennings, ever curious, pressed Margaret to reveal the identity of the young man who held such sway over her sister, Margaret hesitated dramatically. "I must not tell, may I, Elinor?" she asked, glancing sideways at her older sibling.

Of course, this provoked laughter from everyone present, including Elinor, though the effort to smile was painfully strained. She feared Margaret had chosen a suitor whose name she dared not utter in public, lest it become a running gag for the entire gathering.

"Marianne feels deeply for you," the younger girl said, turning crimson with indignation. "But remember, whatever guesses you may make, you have no right to repeat them."

"I never made any conjectures," Margaret retorted, undeterred. "It was you who told me everything."

Her defiance only fueled the amusement of the room. Mrs. Jennings, eager for gossip, pressed further. "Pray, Miss Margaret, let us know all about it. What is the gentleman's name?"

"I cannot tell, ma'am. But I know exactly who he is, and precisely where he resides."

"Yes, yes, we can surely guess," Mrs. Jennings teased. "At his own home at Norland? Perhaps he is the local curate?"

"No, *that* he is not," Margaret corrected sharply. "He holds no profession whatsoever."

"Then perhaps he is deceased," Mrs. Jennings suggested with a mischievous twinkle. "For I am sure there was once a man like him, and his name began with an 'F'."

Just as the conversation teetered on the brink of scandalous speculation, Lady Middleton interjected, "It is raining very hard." Nevertheless, Colonel Brandon, ever attentive to the sensibilities of others, seized upon the topic of rain, engaging Lady Middleton in a lengthy discourse on weather patterns. Meanwhile, Willoughby rose, opening the piano and inviting Marianne to play, effectively burying the subject under music and distraction.

That evening, plans were set for a grand excursion the following day to view the estates of Colonel Brandon's brother-in-law, a property located twelve miles from Barton. What surprised Elinor was not the engagement itself, but how two people of such frank natures could allow themselves to reach this stage without a single word spoken aloud to the outside world.

Her suspicions were confirmed the following day by Margaret. After Willoughby had spent the previous evening with them, leaving the three of them alone in the parlor, Margaret had observed much. Now, with a grave and conspiratorial expression, she confided in Elinor. "Oh, Elinor!" she exclaimed. "I have a secret to tell you about Marianne. I am certain she will be married to Mr. Willoughby very soon."

"You have said so," Elinor replied dryly, "almost every day since they first met on High-church Down. We had not known each other a week before you were convinced Marianne wore his miniature around her neck; yet it turned out to be merely the likeness of our great-uncle."

"But this is entirely different!" Margaret protested, her eyes wide. "He possesses a lock of her hair."

"Eh?" Elinor feigned surprise. "Take care, Margaret. It may simply be a lock of hair from some great-uncle of *his*."

"But truly, Elinor, it is Marianne's!" Margaret insisted, recounting the scene from the previous night with dramatic flair. "Last evening, after tea, when you and Mother stepped out, they were whispering frantically. He seemed to beg something of her, and then he snatched up her scissors. He cut off a long tangle of hair from behind her ear, kissed it reverently, folded it into a white square of paper, and tucked it safely into his pocket-book."

Given the weight of Margaret's testimony and its alignment with what Elinor had witnessed herself, she could not withhold her full belief in the facts.

Yet, Margaret's sharp tongue occasionally betrayed a lack of tact. Later, when Mrs. Jennings, ever curious, pressed Margaret to reveal the identity of the young man who held such sway over her sister, Margaret hesitated dramatically. "I must not tell, may I, Elinor?" she asked, glancing sideways at her older sibling.

Of course, this provoked laughter from everyone present, including Elinor, though the effort to smile was painfully strained. She feared Margaret had chosen a suitor whose name she dared not utter in public, lest it become a running gag for the entire gathering.

"Marianne feels deeply for you," the younger girl said, turning crimson with indignation. "But remember, whatever guesses you may make, you have no right to repeat them."

"I never made any conjectures," Margaret retorted, undeterred. "It was you who told me everything."

Her defiance only fueled the amusement of the room. Mrs. Jennings, eager for gossip, pressed further. "Pray, Miss Margaret, let us know all about it. What is the gentleman's name?"

"I cannot tell, ma'am. But I know exactly who he is, and precisely where he resides."

"Yes, yes, we can surely guess," Mrs. Jennings teased. "At his own home at Norland? Perhaps he is the local curate?"

"No, *that* he is not," Margaret corrected sharply. "He holds no profession whatsoever."

"Then perhaps he is deceased," Mrs. Jennings suggested with a mischievous twinkle. "For I am sure there was once a man like him, and his name began with an 'F'."

Just as the conversation teetered on the brink of scandalous speculation, Lady Middleton interjected, "It is raining very hard." A timely interruption, certainly, though Elinor suspected it stemmed less from kindness toward her sister and more from Lady Middleton's distaste for the kind of raillery that delighted her husband and mother. Nevertheless, Colonel Brandon, ever attentive to the sensibilities of others, seized upon the topic of rain, engaging Lady Middleton in a lengthy discourse on weather patterns. Meanwhile, Willoughby rose, opening the piano and inviting Marianne to play, effectively burying the subject under music and distraction.

That evening, plans were set for a grand excursion the following day to view the estates of Colonel Brandon's brother-in-law, a property located twelve miles from Barton. Access to the grounds required Colonel Brandon's influence, as the owner, currently abroad, had issued strict prohibitions against visitors. The journey was to include a sail on a lake, cold refreshments, and carriage rides, conducted in the customary fashion of a high-society outing. Sir John, a frequent visitor, enthusiastically praised the beauty of the grounds, boasting of his annual trips there for the past decade. However, given the relentless rain of the last fortnight and the precarious state of health suffered by Mrs. Dashwood, who already bore a slight cold, the trip proved somewhat controversial. Persuaded by Elinor's concerns, Mrs. Dashwood ultimately chose to remain at home, sparing herself the damp and exertion of the journey.
